Section on the Selection and Compendium of Matters from the Sūtras Concerning the Factors of Enlightenment (24b). Main Treatise, Chapter Ninety-seven.
Above, there were four explanations of the sūtras; the first three explanations have been concluded. From here below is the fourth.
The *Bodhipakṣadharmavibhāṣā* consists of two fascicles.
It is a compilation that elucidates the essential passages from various sūtras concerning the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*).
It selects and clarifies these key texts.
Among these, first, the preceding section is concluded and the subsequent section is introduced;
second, the verse is cited and explained.
The verse contains both general and specific [explanations].
The summary verse contains ten sections.
The seven categories of the factors of enlightenment constitute seven;
the eighth is mindfulness of breathing.
The ninth is training;
the tenth is verified confidence.
Regarding the detailed explanation:
The major sections are nine;

because the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are explained in one place within the section on the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). First, the foundations of mindfulness are explained.
There are four distinct verses.
The first and fourth each have eight sections,
while the second verse has five sections.
The third verse contains six sections;
together, there are twenty-seven sections.
Regarding the eight sections of the first verse:
First, the śramaṇa;
second, the meaning of śramaṇa;
third, joy and delight.
Fourth, all phenomena;
fifth, the holy life;
sixth, the person.
Seven transcendences;
eight dual defilements.
In the prose section, the first explains the śramaṇa.
First, the four gates are presented in general.
There are śramaṇas who maintain that external phenomena do not exist at all;
subsequently, these four gates will be explained individually.
Regarding this, Master Jing says:
"The place of rest where the one and three fetters are forever severed" refers to the Dharma of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Second, the sphere of the power of the dharma that prevents falling back is the morality concomitant with the path (*mārga-sahabhū-śīla*).
Third, the sphere of the lineage that is certain to lead to enlightenment...
The Buddha is so called.
Those who have attained the stage of "four births at most" or "seven returns at most" are the Sangha.
Regarding those who attain the knowledge of verified clarity (avetyaprasāda) toward the Buddha, Dharma, Saṃgha, and pure ethical discipline based on these four points,
this text states that these four clarities are themselves wisdom (jñāna), not faith (śraddhā).
The Master Da said:
"As for the place of rest,
it lies with the noble ones who abide in the realization of the Path."
Regarding the stage of power (*balasthāna*):
it refers to one who dwells in the fruit of *srotāpanna*. Regarding the category of lineage (*gotrastha*): [it refers to one who abides in the lineage].
Those from the path of accumulation onwards are the noble disciples.
"At most seven returns" refers to those who will be reborn seven times.

This refers to the first type of person: those non-Buddhist teachers who, when confronted with the various forms of grasping (*upādāna*), are unable to establish the correct knowledge of abandonment and full comprehension (*prahāṇa-parijñā*);
yet, they nonetheless proclaim a discourse on the abandonment and full comprehension of all four types of grasping as if they were abandoned.
The second [type]— from "by means of that original bond" onwards—
only severs the grasping for sensual desire (*kāma-upādāna*),
but does not sever the other three.
Third, if one has already abandoned [the afflictions] that are to be abandoned by others and below,
and wishes to attain further abandonment and thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding those previously abandoned.
Fourth, regarding those who possess precepts and observances that are not of the same category as the noble ones:
they have abandoned the first three types of clinging but have not yet abandoned the clinging to a doctrine of self.
This includes all non-Buddhists, who likewise have not abandoned the clinging to a doctrine of self.
This concludes the calculation for the sake of "self.
This is the second explanation of the meaning of *śramaṇa*.
First, three gates are opened to encompass the meaning of *śramaṇa*.
The subsequent question-and-answer section provides a detailed exposition. This consists of two parts;
first, a detailed exposition of the object, the cognition, and the realization.
The subsequent section provides a comprehensive explanation of the three gates that encompass the meaning of *śramaṇa*.
Within this, the first part is divided into three sections.
First, in explaining the objects of focus, four dharmas are extracted from within [the aggregates] to serve as the objects of observation for the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding the statement that the six elements, such as earth and so forth, serve as the substantial basis for the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭ-spraṣṭavyāyatana*):

although the six elements are mentioned, the intention is to regard the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the five elements—excluding space—as the objects of the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
The four great elements and space serve as the basis for the five sense-bases of contact, such as the eye;
the consciousness element serves as the basis for the mind-base of contact;
and the six bases of contact serve as the basis for the eighteen mental explorations.
Regarding the basis: although the six bases of contact, such as the eye and so forth, are mentioned,
the intention is to take the essence of contact produced by the six faculties as the object of the application of mindfulness of dharmas.
From those six sense faculties arise painful contact, pleasant contact, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact.
The arising of the six types of grief, the six types of joy, and the six types of equanimity constitutes the object of the mindfulness foundation of feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
These eighteen mental explorations (*manopavicāra*) defile the simultaneously arising mind-king, and thus constitute the mindfulness foundation of the mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Next, the explanation of wisdom refers to the pure mind taking superior insight (*adhiprajñā*) as its basis.
In the subsequent explanation of realization,
first, the question and answer cite four points.
Next, the four bases are explained through questions and answers,
followed by a general analysis.
These four bases of reliance are also called the four virtuous bases (*caturguṇavastu*).

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* identifies four masters as the basis for the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, however, explains the four reliances by correlating them specifically with the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
It designates the first, second, and third stages as the "stages based on the truths" (*satya-bhūmi-pratisaraṇa*).
The fourth, fifth, and sixth stages are called the Stage of Reliance on Wisdom;
the seventh and eighth stages are called the Stage of Equanimity;
and the ninth, tenth, and eleventh stages are called the Stage of Quiescence.
In this present passage, the basis upon which wisdom relies is first clarified:
it is cultivated and attained on the stage of ordinary beings prior to the path of vision,
and continues from the entry into the path of vision up to the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, after supramundane wisdom has been accomplished, there is mundane wisdom.
If one relies upon the truths as the basis,
then by means of the Eightfold Noble Path already attained, one abandons all afflictions and realizes arhatship.
Because all sufferings do not arise and there is no delusion or loss,
it is called the basis of truth (*satyāśraya*).
As for the basis of equanimity (*upekṣāśraya*):
Regarding the basis for tranquility, which consists of dwelling in happiness in the present life through conduct free from affliction with respect to matters already abandoned,
it is for one who diligently practices the means to abandon the remaining fetters.
Having already attained the Path of Seeing, one proceeds to abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). This refers to specific instances,
as in the passage beginning with "having already attained the Path," and so forth.
This is the general classification.
To summarize all of this: for one who cultivates wisdom in order to attain realization, that which serves as the basis for the cultivation of wisdom is [the object].
Regarding the statement, "Having attained realization, one then obtains the noble path and the fruit of the noble path":
"attaining realization" refers precisely to the basis of the truths.
He then attains the noble path;
this is the third [fruit], by which,
through the abandonment of defilements, he attains dwelling in happiness in the present life.
And that which pertains to the fruit of the noble path is the fourth,
because it relies upon tranquility.
By extinguishing the remaining fetters, one attains the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
From this point on, the following section provides a detailed analysis of the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*).
The first [section] distinguishes the matured [state];
next, it explains it;
and with "In this way," and so forth, it concludes.
In this context, the noble path previously obtained and termed the "path of tranquility" refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It is for the purpose of abandoning the afflictions of the higher stages.

In order to eliminate the afflictions of the stage of cultivation, one applies oneself doubly to the severance of those specific objects; this refers to the severance of karma and its retribution, which serves to prevent a fall from what has already been attained regarding the abandonment of the afflictions.
Regarding the abandonment of afflictions, this prevents falling away from what has been attained but not yet fully realized.
Above, the realization of the objects and wisdom of individual liberation was explained separately;
below, through a series of questions and answers, the three gates are comprehensively distinguished as they encompass the meaning of the *śramaṇa*.
"Referring to those from right application up to the point where there is no self at all.
Master Jing says:
"This refers to the stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)."
One separately contemplates the emptiness of the four great elements internally and externally.
Abiding in the five stages, one practices the contemplation of the body;
for the sake of seeking superior right wisdom and the two liberations, one contemplates the selflessness of the elements.
This is precisely the intent of giving rise to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
For one who, by the power of analytical investigation (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), has already become free from craving for the various realms of form (*rūpadhātu*),
this refers to suppression and abandonment.
As for those who have not yet been able to sever [defilements] with respect to the objects of perception,
they have not severed the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This refers to the future and the lower realms.
Regarding the refutation of the reason why [the fetters] are not severed:
as for "liberation of the mind" and so forth,
it is because of being free from greed that the mind attains liberation.
From this point until "observing without error," observing the five internal sense faculties constitutes the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). From here below,
observing sensation constitutes the foundation of mindfulness of sensation (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding the phrase "also free from greed and so forth toward the realm of all feelings," this refers to observing defiled feelings.
Because they have already distanced themselves from ignorance, they possess the predominant power of liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
Liberation is attained through wisdom that is free from ignorance.

This contemplation of pure feeling takes as its object all wholesome feelings associated with appropriate attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) arising from contact with clarity (*vidyā-saṃsparśaja*). This constitutes the mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
From this point onward,
regarding the eighteen mental explorations up to the cultivation of the contemplation of mental phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā*),
it is summarized that the mindfulness of feeling constitutes the contemplation of mental phenomena.
He reflects thus: "Among these eighteen mental explorations, the foremost is the equanimity of the formless realm.

If one becomes attached to this equanimity—whether through meditative absorption or birth—and dwells on it with recollection, the mind becomes defiled. Having understood this, he relinquishes it and does not dwell on it, abiding instead in the contemplation of the mind as it occurs.
Knowing and recollecting the faults of superior feelings, one abandons them and contemplates the mind; this is called the mindfulness-establishment of the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Furthermore, contemplating the nature of impermanence within all sense bases is called the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), wherein one cultivates the contemplation of phenomena; the rest is as previously explained.
The three lower emptinesses are called the three meditative absorptions of perception (saṃjñā-samādhi),
as well as the perception of compassion (karuṇā-saṃjñā).
Merely suppressing and departing from greed is termed "attaining detachment" (viveka-lābha).
The inability to sever the seeds is as previously described.
That which is attained by the noble ones (*ārya*)— the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)— is able to sever the seeds of craving.
Ordinary persons attain a state of non-perception,
yet they merely suppress their craving and cannot permanently sever it; therefore,
it is said that those who have already abandoned craving for the "peak of existence" (bhavāgra) and so forth are distinct from them.
The above clarifies how ordinary persons practice the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness;
the following distinguishes how those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) practice the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness. Master Da says:
Regarding the "five elements," these are the five internal sense-faculty elements.
Regarding the "four kinds of craving":
Greed for gain, honor, and fame is attachment.
The four kinds of ill will are hatred toward loss, defamation, suffering, and censure.
Third is the explanation of the gate of joy and bliss.
This refers to attaining joy, bliss, and so forth by cultivating the seven wholesome dharmas.
Within this, there are two parts.
First, the seven true dharmas as conditions are correctly explained;
subsequently, it is clarified that by practicing the seven wholesome dharmas, one attains two benefits.
Within the former [section]:
First, the opening chapter lists the names;
second, the detailed explanation.
Within the former:
Because it is the object of the attention consisting of what is heard (*śrutamaya-manasikāra*),
it is established as "knowledge of the Dharma" (*dharmajñāna*); for one is able to know the Dharma by means of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Because the two types of cultivation— reflection and meditative development— take the two types of mental attention as their objects,
they are established as "knowing the meaning.
This is because these two forms of wisdom are able to know that meaning.
Third, these three types of mental attention are established as "knowing the time" because they differ according to the specific mode of practice; that is,
the three types of wisdom are able to know the time.
When restlessness arises, one uses calm abiding (*śamatha*) to subdue it;
when dullness arises, one uses the uplifting of wisdom (*prajñā-utsāha*) to subdue it;
and when ignorance arises, one uses equanimity (*upekṣā*) to subdue it.
Therefore, it is said that one "knows the time.
Fourth, because one skillfully and thoroughly understands the enjoyment of wealth and the universal enjoyment of wealth,
the designation "knowing the measure" is established.
This means that because one who enjoys wealth thoroughly enjoys riches and is well-versed in them, it is so called.
Fifth, the enjoyment of wealth and Dharma is obtained from others from time to time.
Therefore, the "knowledge of assemblies" is established; that is, skillfully knowing the various groups of people,
such as who is the king, who is the minister, and who are those of respectful faith, and so forth.
Because others receive [the teaching].
Sixth, at the time of culmination, one is internally free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and thus remains undegenerated;
hence, one establishes self-knowledge as the seventh. Furthermore, one is also free from overweening pride toward others and remains undegenerated.
Therefore, the knowledge of the relative rank [of beings] is established.
From this point downward is the second explanation.
Among the seven causal conditions, the first two are not explained here,
as they have already been explained in various places previously. As for the third:
"Refers to the Śrāvaka-bhūmi.
Regarding "the fourth," it refers to the Śrāvaka-bhūmi.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "In this regard, those who enjoy material wealth" explains the fifth [point], knowing the assembly.
The passage beginning with "I should practice in this manner" [explains the sixth].

The section beginning with "Furthermore, preceded by faith" explains the sixth [topic], self-knowledge. The section beginning with "Furthermore, having first established faith" explains the seventh [topic], knowing the noble and the humble.
Regarding these five dharmas: faith comes first, followed by the single dharma of upholding the precepts.
First is the observance of ethical discipline;
second is the pursuit of extensive learning,
which is preceded by that [observance].
Abandoning the three faults and so forth;
with this as the precursor, the mind attains calm concentration (samatha). 4.
Regarding the five [aspects] of realizing wisdom as it truly is,
the statement "briefly, there are two types of persons" is a dual designation.
Regarding the two types:
first, the noble; second, the base.
These two types are the distinction between the two types.
"Returning to the discrimination between the noble and the base"—
one should know that these two being "superior" refers to the discernment of the distinction between those two types of persons;
it means returning to discern the difference between the aforementioned two individuals.
The following clarifies that by practicing the seven virtues, one attains two benefits:
first, joy and happiness;
second, the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
The fourth section explains all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
First, it distinguishes how the trainings (*śikṣā*) and the fruits of training encompass all phenomena;
subsequently, it distinguishes how the trainings and the fruits of training constitute the provisions for realization that remedy the eight faults.
Regarding the preceding middle section:

it is said that by the predominant power of hearing the true Dharma, one is able to swiftly accumulate and realize the contact of the light of higher knowledge (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*); therefore, that is described as the accumulation of contact.
Through hearing the true Dharma, one is able to realize and directly experience [the truth];
thus, it is said that hearing the Dharma constitutes the origination of contact.
This "contact of clarity" (vidyā-sparśa) is untainted contact (anāsrava-sparśa).
In truth, it is not that speech is uttered to clarify contact and thus name it "designation" (*adhivacana*);
rather, it is called "designation" because it is the remote condition for the utterance of speech.
Furthermore, this clarifying contact (*vibhūta-sparśa*) encompasses both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Now, what is called "contact of clear illumination" (*ālokasaṃsparśa*) refers to that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*).

Furthermore, because all outflows have been eternally exhausted, one attains liberation accompanied by feeling born from contact of ultimate clear illumination (*atyantālokasaṃsparśaja-vedanā-sahagata-vimukti*).
The nirvāṇa realized at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is called liberation.
This very liberation is "up to the nature of being faultless" because it is the foremost among the bliss of the cessation of nirvāṇa.
The subsequent passage states that "liberation is firm," which refers to the realm of nirvana with remainder; thus,
one knows that liberation is unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*).
Below, [the text] explains the training, the fruits of training, the requisites for realization, and the cultivation of the nine perceptions as remedies for the eight faults.
Regarding the eight faults:
first is attachment to gain and honor.
1. Attachment to all formations pertaining to future existence; 2.
Laziness and indolence; 3.
The view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
1. Attachment to delicious flavors; 2–5.
[The four types of craving] up to craving for existence within the various worlds; 6. Craving for sensual pleasure;
7. Resorting to negligence and the means of unwholesome conduct.
There are eight [faults] consisting of practicing the holy life based on wrong aspirations;
these eight defects are that which is to be remedied,
while the nine perceptions are the remedy.
Master Jing said:
"Among the nine contemplations, once each has been able to remedy the eight faults,
the final two contemplations are difficult to understand."
In his own critical analysis of the treatise,
Master Da states:
"The fifth and sixth perceptions together counteract the fifth [affliction], which is attachment to delicious flavors."
The remaining seven perceptions are called the remedies for a single fault;
this can be understood from their initial sequence.
The fifth [section] explains the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Regarding the statement, "Because one does not know these three points as they truly are," etc., these are:
first, the outflows (*āsrava*); second, the sensations (*vedanā*); and third, wrong conceptions (*mithyā-saṃjñā*).
Regarding the first five stations of the truths (*satyasthāna*):
first, the various outflows (*āsrava*);
second, the feeling of ignorance (*avidyāvedanā*).
Third, wrong conceptions;
fourth, various desires;
fifth, karma leading to future existence.
Among these five, one does not know them as they truly are.
Regarding the last one, which pertains to the Truth of Suffering,
one does not know those manifold sufferings as they truly are.
Sixth, the explanation of the *pudgala*.
First, a general presentation;
second, a detailed explanation.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the six types of persons;
second, the explanation of how the Buddha’s wisdom knows reality as it truly is.
The preceding section is further divided into two parts:
first, the identification of the six types of persons;
second, a re-examination of their meaning.
Regarding the preceding section: first, the first three [categories] are distinguished;
next, they are concluded.
The latter two will be explained later;
they are simply the reversal of the former.
Within the section on the detailed explanation of the meaning:
If one places the wholesome dharmas of previous lives into the midst of the evil teachings and the extinction of the Dharma in the present life, causing those wholesome qualities to diminish,
it is like placing hot coals upon cold ground or within a stone vessel, thereby causing the coals to lose their heat.
If one takes the wholesome dharmas of previous lives and places them within the well-expounded Dharma to practice them again,
it is like placing hot coals inside a dry reed hut, causing the charcoal fire to blaze fiercely.
The seventh section is the explanation of transcendence (*atikrama*). First, the five gates are presented in summary regarding the thorough knowledge of transcendence;
next, the five gates are explained individually.
Subsequently, these are combined to form two "transcendental" categories (*atikrānta*). Within the detailed explanation,
the first interpretation includes one gate.
Next, the remaining four gates will be explained.
Within the preceding section, there are three parts;
first, the conduct leading to rebirth in the evil destinies is analyzed.
Next, the gate of permanent impairment is distinguished;
finally, the gate of thorough knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-parijñā*) is distinguished.
Among these, the remaining four gates are explained.
First, the four gates are distinguished;
subsequently, the universal knowledge of the Buddha and others is distinguished.
As for the gate of upward progression:
Master Jing said:
"The last of the superior-class *anāgāmins* takes the attainment of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception as their ultimate goal."
Now, the explanation of "subsequent" (*paścāt*) refers to what is present before one,
not to the very last [moment].
The eighth [section] explains the two defilements.
First, there is a brief comparative analysis of the two types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) as their antidotes;
subsequently, they will be explained extensively according to their meaning.
Regarding the former:
Master Jing’s commentary explains:
"The noble disciples who have even attained entry into the immovable, non-existent, and non-percipient meditative absorptions" refers to the four dhyānas and the two lower formless attainments.
This is also called the "immovable concentration" (*aniñjya-samādhi*).
Severing the desires of the desire realm through the nine stages of non-obstruction (*ānantarya*) and the eight stages of liberation (*vimokṣa*) is termed "proceeding toward the first dhyāna.
It is the practice of immovable concentration that is free from external distraction and the desires [of the lower realms].
Transcending the nine stages of the unhindered paths and eight liberations of the first dhyāna is called "proceeding toward the second dhyāna";
it is the practice of immovability that is free from the movement of applied and sustained thought.

The nine paths of non-obstruction and eight paths of liberation for transcending the second dhyāna are called "the path leading to the third dhyāna," which is the immovable practice free from the agitation of joy.
Detaching from the desires of the third dhyāna through nine paths of non-obstruction and eight liberations is called "proceeding toward the fourth dhyāna.
It is the unshakable practice that is free from being moved by pleasure.
Having abandoned the desires of the four dhyānas, there are nine unimpeded concentrations and eight liberations;
these are called the progression toward the sphere of infinite space.
They consist of perceptions of variegated colors, perceptions of resistance, perceptions of various distinctions, and the movements of both motion and non-motion.

When one is free from desire for the sphere of infinite space, during the nine stages of the unhindered knowledges (*ānantarya*) and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), this is called "proceeding toward the sphere of infinite consciousness.
One is thus freed from those movements and non-movements of the external objects and gates associated with the sphere of infinite space.
Taking the sign of emptiness externally within the sphere of infinite space is called movement of the external door;
in the sphere of infinite consciousness, one internally takes consciousness as an object.
It is called "the Immovable.
When one is free from the sphere of consciousness and abides in the nine stages of non-obstruction and the eight liberations,
it is called "proceeding toward the practice of nothingness."
Detaching from the desire realm, the four dhyānas, and the sphere of infinite space,
it is called the attainment of the ninth liberation and the realization of the immovable concentration.
Detaching from the sphere of infinite consciousness, it is the ninth liberation.
This is called the realization of entry into the concentration of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*).
Departing from the ninth liberation of nothingness,
it is called the realization of entry into the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
It is said that one transcends desire and becomes free from attachment through the counteractive of abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*) and the counteractive of distancing (*dūribhāvapratipakṣa*).
The first dhyāna is the counteractive of abandonment for the defilements associated with desire.
The second dhyāna and above, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, are collectively termed the "distant antidote" (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*).
Alternatively, they are for the purpose of abandoning the defilements of future existence, thinking: "When shall I no longer exist?"
Because of the suffering of birth and so forth, one says, "I have suffering.
Thinking, "When will my suffering no longer exist?
one says, "When will that which belongs to me (mamakāra) no longer exist?"
One takes birth and the other forms of suffering as the very substance of the self.
Since such a self of suffering will inevitably exist, one asks, "When shall this self not exist? Hence, it is said: "When shall I not exist?"

Regarding the statement, "I shall not exist, and what belongs to me shall not exist," this arises from the prior application of right effort directed toward the mind that experiences the suffering of the cessation of pleasure;
having applied such right effort, one attains the various distinctions of the preceding and succeeding meditative concentrations.
By this cause and condition, he further attains certainty, namely:
"Suffering shall not exist for me, nor shall there be anything belonging to me that is suffering.
He says: "Whether it be what exists now or what existed in the past, I shall relinquish it all."
The various karmas currently being created are called "those belonging to the present," while all other past karmas are called "those belonging to the past.
One does not seek the retributive fruits of either of these two types of karma.
They are all termed "abandonment.
When one correctly practices until reaching the ability to enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, through that correct practice,
one is able to sever the distinctions between the prior and subsequent states of the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments of existence.
The following clarifies that while common liberation is attained by both ordinary beings and noble ones, noble liberation alone pertains to the latter;
the afflictive obstructions of the eight lower stages are abandoned by both ordinary beings and noble ones alike.
Although the methods of subduing and severing [the afflictions] differ,

speaking of them in general terms, the unconditioned state of the eighth stage is called "common liberation," whereas the analytical cessation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is exclusively "noble liberation."
Thus, there are five locations in total, up to and including the fifth, the noble liberation.
The preceding text mentioned only the progression toward immovable conduct and the progression toward nothingness.
It does not say that one proceeds to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; rather, it says here that one proceeds to nirvana in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is identical in substance to the noble liberation, though differing in its specific meaning.
The Master Da said:
"The preceding text must be incomplete;
it should state 'proceeding to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception' in full."
The subsequent text contains this in full;
what follows provides a detailed analysis according to the meaning.
First, it clarifies the faults and afflictions of the defilement of desire.
Secondly, having further explained the mind of superior skillful means that is free from higher desire, it is called "vast. Below, the observation of subsequent defilement is clarified.
As for the statement, "Furthermore, by means of wisdom... one shall certainly go to the immovable state in the future," [it refers to this].
This is discussed with reference to one whose body resides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, for three reasons, these stages are established as "unshakable" (*āniñjya*):

from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), there are three causal conditions for establishing them as unshakable; the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) associated with these conditions extend all the way up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Therefore, all concentrations from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of consciousness (vijñānāyatana) are termed "concentrations with something superior" (sopadhika-samādhi);
the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), however, is the concentration without anything superior (anupadhika-samādhi).
From this point upward, it is further called the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception attainment" (asaṃjñāsaṃjñāyatana).
Thus, by means of three parts, the three modes of practice are taught;
that is, the three modes of practice are taught by way of three causal divisions.

That is to say, by means of the factors of the immovable concentration (*āneñjya-samādhi*), the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one proclaims the practice of the immovable, the practice of nothingness, and the practice of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Through these three gateways, the noble disciples are established as those who proceed toward the three immovable practices.
Thus, because one is weary of the distraction of external desires, one establishes the practice of immovability directed toward the first dhyāna;
because one is weary of the distractions of vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha, one establishes the practice of immovability directed toward the fourth dhyāna.

Because one becomes weary of the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) and perceptions of resistance (*pratigha-saṃjñā*), etc., one establishes the practice of proceeding toward emptiness (*ākāśa*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the immovable (*āniñjya*).
Furthermore, from the perception of form up to this point, it is called the first practice of proceeding toward nothingness (*ākiṃcanya*).

Having recently become weary of the perception of form arising from the fourth dhyāna, one next becomes weary of the perceptions of the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness, as well as the perception of imperturbability; this deep sense of weariness and destruction constitutes the first approach to the practice of nothingness.
Furthermore, in this very context, up to what is called "the practitioner of the second course":
first is the "surpassable," which refers to the practice of impermanence;
second is the "unsurpassable," which refers solely to the practice of non-self.
Because there is something superior, one enters this meditative absorption by wearying of and destroying the lower stages.
Because there is nothing superior, one enters the state of non-existence by contemplating the selflessness of all phenomena in both the lower and upper stages.
This supreme practice is called the second entry into the practice of non-existence (*akiṃcanya*).
It is that which relies on the wisdom of selflessness, up to the point where there is nothing to which one belongs.
Just as I do not belong to another, so too another does not belong to me.
As for the statement, "Furthermore, in this context, when will 'mine' not exist? and so forth,
this explains the preceding passage,
which has already been fully interpreted.
In the second verse, there are five sections:

Third, the explanation of the nature of obstacles during the time of cultivation;

Within the first section on "Understanding," first is the understanding of the formal establishment;

Third, the explanation of purity.
Within this, first is the explanation of what constitutes purity.
Regarding the phrase "paths or objects of focus that are dissimilar," this refers to the paths and objects of focus as conceived by non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*). From here on,
the second section provides a detailed explanation of the meaning of the phrases within the sutra.
Regarding the statement that sorrow takes the four worldly conditions as its basis:
these are ruin, decline, disparagement, and suffering.
The second explanation concerns the dependent origination of reality (*yoniśaḥ-pratītyasamutpāda*).
The meaning can be understood by consulting the text.
The third section explains the nature of the obstacles during the time of cultivation.
Regarding the statement that "the first [verse] provides a general heading":
This is interesting.
Regarding the separate explanations of the latter three,

The fourth is the explanation of abandonment,
as in the text.
The fifth is the explanation of the cultivation of arising.
One attains mastery over the three antidotes as desired—

and dwells with perceptions of revulsion and so forth toward agreeable and other objects.
Cultivating revulsion toward agreeable objects such as the body is the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*).
The phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to cultivating the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward the four disagreeable objects, such as the body, and so on.
The abandonment of those two types— equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension—
is precisely the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
In the third verse, there are six sections.
First, the sense faculties;
second, the relish for flavors;

Fourth, the signs;
fifth, the various fetters;
sixth, the great fruits and benefits.
In the explanation of the first gate,
it is said that "the root of a single unwholesome action can cause one to dwell in the suffering of the evil destinies in the future.
This means that unwholesome actions of body and so forth serve as the root for the suffering of the evil destinies.
The three roots of sensual desire, ill will,
and harmfulness serve as the roots for the three types of discursive thought— sensual desire and so forth;
these two constitute a double root.
Desire, ill-will, and harmfulness serve as roots for the three realms, as well as for the three roots of greed and so forth, and the three roots of desire and so forth;
these are the threefold roots.
Second is the explanation of the relish of craving (*āsvāda*).
"By means of the worldly path, up to not diligently seeking [the supramundane]," etc.

This passage is the same as what is stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*: that the mundane path cannot suppress or subdue the afflictions such as craving for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The third explains the distinction between the preceding and succeeding [states],
because one thoroughly understands the distinction between the preceding and succeeding states of the mind that has not yet attained liberation and the mind that has attained liberation.

The statement here that "the steward of the kitchen" up to "exquisite food and clothing" is a metaphor for internal *śamatha* and so forth;

The preparation of offerings for the master is analogous to the practitioner of yoga;
the ritual implements for settling and uplifting are similar to the mind embraced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
and the side dishes are a metaphor for the signs of settling and uplifting.
The essential nature of concentration is precisely its ability to nourish the simultaneously arising mind-king,
just as superior clothing and food do;
the categories of "black" and "white" are metaphors for the ignorant and the wise, respectively.
The fifth concerns the various fetters (paryavasthāna);
the sixth concerns the benefits (anuśaṃsa).
These may be understood according to the text.
In the ninety-eighth fascicle, within the section on the Foundations of Mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the fourth verse has eight sections:

This is an analogy for the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣabhūmi*). As for the statement, "Furthermore, all foolish commoners must observe other objects until they fail to attain liberation," this refers to ordinary persons who,

Seeking a higher realm from a lower one, and so on,
until one still fails to attain liberation within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—

Regarding the four meanings established:

Regarding the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*):

Are the Arhats,

This is the fifth explanation of the gradual sequence.
As for householders, they possess only pure faith and purification from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), lacking the three gradual stages of the intermediate [stages]. The sixth [section],
the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-paripūri*),
may be understood accordingly.
Seventh is the virtue of explanation.
Regarding the statement, "One should know that the desire realm is like the skin and so forth," this means that the human body is used as a metaphor for the three realms.
The desire realm is like the skin;
the higher realms are like the flesh;
and ignorance within the flesh is like the blood.
This is because within the bodies of the three realms, there are outflows such as the blood of ignorance.
The eighth [section], the accomplishment of liberation,
may be understood from the text as it stands.
The second major section: Explaining the Right Exertions (*samyakprahāṇa*) and the Bases of Psychic Power (*ṛddhipāda*).
A half-verse enumerates their five categories.
First, courage;
second, strength;
third, the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The four alternative formulations and the five bases of supernormal power;
the first is the gate of valor.
He elucidates the four right efforts,
the four bases of power, and so forth,
and distinguishes the four bases of supernormal power.
In the prose commentary,
the "Gate of Valor" is explained first.
Herein, the fifth phrase concerning valor is proclaimed.
Vigor consists of five phrases.
First, from "armor-like vigor" up to the fifth, "not relinquishing the noble yoke," these constitute valor.
Second is the power of understanding.

To speak briefly, the four powers sustain the mind so that it becomes concentrated; they sustain it even within meditative absorption (*samādhi*). There is only this much work to be done by meditative absorption, and nothing beyond or in addition to this.

Apart from the removal of desire, the advancement of mind and wisdom, and the four powers, there is no other cause or condition for seeking meditative concentration (samādhi), whether by surpassing or exceeding [these].
This is the third explanation of the cultivation of samādhi.
Master Jing’s commentary states:
Regarding "desire and so forth":
these refer to desire, diligence, mind, and wisdom that function in conjunction with indolence;
hence they are called "desire and so forth."
Regarding the statement that "the objects of focus for the category of vipaśyanā are the 'preceding and succeeding perceptions'":

this refers to the mutual entry of the preceding and succeeding characteristics during the cultivation of the four types of knowledge—those arising from hearing, reflection, meditation, and realization—which is termed "preceding and succeeding perceptions."
Regarding the objects of focus for the *śamatha* section: these are the perceptions of "above" and "below," and so forth, as well as the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
Entering from a lower stage into a higher stage is termed the perception of "above" and "below."

Regarding the objects of focus for the "concomitant" category: for a practitioner who cultivates the mind until it proceeds in conjunction with various light-images, when first practicing observation, they produce the sign of luminosity.
At that time, there is a portion of the light-image that arises within the mind and serves as the object of focus.
To briefly examine this below:
A question is asked:
"Desire, diligence, and so forth are wholesome dharmas."
How can it be associated with and coexist with indolence?
Therefore, the treatise itself explains: "Furthermore, it is not like desire and so forth," up until it says, "it is called that which coexists with indolence."
Because diligence cannot be continuous and is interspersed with indolence, it is called "concomitant.
Furthermore, these five characteristics should be understood as collectively encompassing all types of cultivation and so forth.
The characteristics of the cultivation of the supernormal power of the five causal conditions,
as explained here, encompass all types of methods for cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*) such as joy.
Through this cultivation, meditative concentration is swiftly perfected.
Now, examining the second and eighth fascicles, regarding the "Chapter on Cessation" (Zhipin), it says:
"The perception of upper and lower refers to observing this body as it is situated,
according to its location, from the crown of the head above down to the soles of the feet below."
It is filled with various kinds of impurities.

Regarding the meditative visualization of the preceding and succeeding stages of the "Contemplation Chapter" (Vipaśyanā-bhūmi), it refers to a case where someone, with respect to the object of contemplation, [proceeds as follows].
With earnestness and sincerity, one skillfully grasps, skillfully contemplates, skillfully understands, and skillfully penetrates [the truth].
That is to say, while standing one observes while sitting, while sitting one observes while lying down;
or, while walking behind, one observes those walking ahead.
As explained extensively therein, the fourth [section] provides an alternative interpretation (*paryāya*).
Furthermore, regarding the "five bases of liberation" (*pañca-vimukti-sthāna*) and so forth, it is as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
First, one attains liberation by listening to the Dharma;
second, one attains liberation by teaching it to others;
third, one attains liberation by personally reciting and chanting the sutras.
Fourth, one attains liberation through reflection on causes.
Fifth, one attains liberation through practice in accordance with the Dharma.
If there is a bhikṣu who, relying on pure intention and intense aspiration, reaches what is called the "desire-samādhi."
This refers to attaining concentration through listening to the Dharma.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who has attained what is called the samādhi of diligence;
this refers to attaining concentration through two means: teaching others and reciting for oneself.
These combined constitute the samādhi of diligence.
Furthermore, there is that which is called the "mind samādhi" (citta-samādhi);
this arises from the samādhi produced by one's own contemplation of signs such as impurity.
It is called the "Concentration on the Mind" because it grasps the king of the mind.
Furthermore, there are others up to and including what is called the "Concentration on Contemplation," which is attained through practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipatti).
The practice of discerning abandonment is precisely the provisions for the eight cessations;
it is the fifth, the supernormal power of resolve.
The term "impure caste individuals" refers to those who belong solely to the internal Dharma;
the *caṇḍāla* caste is called an impure category of beings.
It should be known that those of this class can cultivate the various noble bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) only by abiding in the internal Dharma.
Regarding the noble ones who manifest supernormal powers (*abhijñā*),
there are four such powers.
First, transformation;
second, the alteration of nature, which changes its inherent character;
third, the duration of abiding.
Regarding the fourth transformation, the textual characteristics are easily understood.
This concludes the third major section: the explanation of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
There is one verse that enumerates its four gates:
first, the establishment;
second, the objective sphere of activity.
One should know that the three faculties of wisdom are supreme and are established as the final [stage].
Regarding the four external categories of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth,
this concludes the initial exposition on the gateway of establishment.
Having distinguished the five faculties beginning with faith,
one has thereby distinguished the remaining twenty-two faculties.
Second, the objects of their activity are explained.
Regarding "arising from clarity and liberation":
untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is termed "clarity" (*vidyā*),
and the factor of liberation (*vimukti*) associated with that wisdom is termed "liberation" (*mokṣa*).
The third [section] explains the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) up to its firm abiding;
it may be understood according to the text.
The fourth [section] explains the category of external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjanapakṣa*) and so forth.
That is to say, if one lacks the five faculties such as faith in the Buddha,
one is merely an external worldling (bāhyapṛthagjana).
If one possesses only the mundane (laukika) five faculties such as faith regarding enlightenment (bodhi), [one is likewise an external worldling].
These are internal ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
If they give rise to untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) toward enlightenment,
they are designated as the category of noble ones (*ārya*).
It is not of that category.
The fourth major section explains the five powers (*pañcabala*).
There is one verse that enumerates its six gates.
First, analytical investigation;
second, awakening wisdom and so forth;
third, kingdoms and so forth, as well as various kings.
1. The four types of arhats; 2. the five types of those in training (śaikṣa);
3. the straightforward (rjuka).
In the prose commentary,
the first two sections are clear;
the third explains the king and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "Based on the country and the king, up to the ten powers (*daśabala*) and so forth," some masters explain that the ten powers are established because one possesses sovereign power over the country and other such domains; this should be further examined.
Now it is explained:
first, the kingdom and so forth;
second, the king.
Up to and including the tenth, the community of renunciants;
based on these ten types,
the ten powers (daśabala) are established.

Fourth is the interpretation of the arhat.

there are two powers concerning the non-creation of unwholesome karma.
First, one does not create it because of revulsion toward future existence.
Second, because one feels revulsion toward all desires, one does not create [karmic actions].
Within the cultivation of wholesome states, there are six powers,
namely the seven stages of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa).
The two categories of faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) are combined into one;
thus, there are six. Now, the explanation follows.
The right abandonments (samyakprahāṇa) and the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) are combined into one; thus, there are six.
The fifth [section] explains those in training (śaikṣa).
Regarding those trainees who have accomplished the five powers,

"Ask further."
Now, examining the one hundredth fascicle, it says:
"Based on the Vinaya, a bhikṣu who diligently trains accomplishes five powers:
first, the power of application."
Second, the power of intention;
third, the power of elucidation;
fourth, the power of correct knowledge.
The fifth is the power of straightforwardness.
Regarding the two causes and conditions,
the first is the fulfillment of one's own practice.
Second, benefiting others is for one's own benefit.
The sixth section, "Resolving on Uprightness and so forth," is clear in its text.
The fifth major section explains the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
There is one verse that enumerates its seven categories, the first of which is their establishment.
Second, the distinctions;
third, the sustenances;
fourth, the gradual sequence.
Fifth, peace and happiness;
sixth, abiding;
seventh, cultivation.
First, regarding the explanation of establishing the gates:
as for "based on śamatha," the triad of concentration (*samādhi*),
tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) constitutes śamatha.
The section on *vipaśyanā* concerns the vigor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-vīrya*).
The section associated with joy concerns...
Mindfulness pervades both parts.
Second is the explanation of their distinctions,
which should be verified against the preceding text.
There is an interpretation that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of the seven objects of focus (*ālambana*), which are established based on four causal conditions (*pratyaya*).
The following three gates can be understood [by this].
The sixth is the gate of abiding (*sthiti*).
Regarding the statement that one abides in four factors of enlightenment during the first watch:
these are concentration, tranquility, equanimity, and mindfulness.
Regarding those who abide in four factors of enlightenment during the second watch:
Regarding the one who fully dwells in the seven factors of enlightenment during the third watch— namely, the investigation of phenomena, vigor, joy, and mindfulness—
one possesses both the portions of concentration and wisdom, being complete in all seven factors of enlightenment, rather than dwelling in only a single factor of enlightenment.
The Master Da said:
"This means that the awakening factor of mindfulness is the very beginning of cultivation.
Furthermore, it explains that there has never been one who practiced otherwise."
"Abiding solely in one awakening factor. This is the seventh explanation, the section on cultivation.
Master Jing says:
"Regarding the explanation of the twenty-one perceptions..."
First, the perception of impermanence;
second, the perception of suffering;
third, the perception of non-self.
Fourth, the perception of emptiness;
fifth, the perception of impurity;
sixth, the perception of revulsion toward food.
7. The perception of the world as unpleasurable;
8. The perception of enmity;
9. The perception of cessation.
Tenth is the perception of detachment;
eleventh is the perception of cessation.
Following these are the nine perceptions of contemplation.
The initial contemplation is on a corpse turning blue-black;
emptiness is the final.
This has been verified by consulting the scriptural text.
These are recorded herein;
furthermore, adding the characteristic of disadvantage makes twenty-one.
As for the statement that one [characteristic] is based on the meaning of association and co-occurrence:
This is simultaneously associated with the seven factors of enlightenment;
that is, the cultivation of the perception of impermanence and so forth, up to the cultivation of the perception of death.
This is based on the fact that such contemplative practice is performed within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of an already realized noble one (*ārya*).
It is associated with the seven factors of enlightenment.
Second, it is based on the sense of uninterrupted co-occurrence;
that is, from the perception of impurity up to the perception of contemplating emptiness.

This refers to practicing the contemplation of impurity within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), continuing until one contemplates nothing but the skeletal remains and empties the mind and consciousness;

this is what is meant by "entering into the seven factors of enlightenment in succession," which is the sense of being based upon the immediate path (*ānantarya-mārga*). The same applies to loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].
This general example does not imply that the contemplations of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth are included within the enumeration of the twenty-one types of thought.
Next, the obstacles to be remedied by these twenty-one types of thought are explained;
there are fourteen such obstacles.
First, attachment and defilement within the activities of the three periods of time;
second, falling into indolence;

and third, although the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) has been extinguished, its habitual tendencies continue to bind one, and the manifestation of the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) persists.
Fourth, craving for the taste of sensory objects;
fifth, craving for the exquisite things of the world;
sixth, the remaining latent afflictions (*anuśaya*).
Seventh, the seeking of gain and offerings;
eighth, the seeking of livelihood;
ninth, if there are cravings for sensual desires.
Tenth, if there is craving,
or if one follows false conceptualization,
there are further four kinds of sensual desire.
First, greed for beauty;
second, greed for physical form;
third, greed for subtle touch.
Fourth is the craving for service.
Thus, up to the point of "proceeding by deviating from the path," the faults of these obstacles are analyzed.

To counteract those [obstacles], there are twenty-one distinct modes of cultivating the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) accompanied by their respective mental applications (saṃjñā), as appropriate;
these are intended to serve as antidotes based on the correspondence of their objects, rather than according to a fixed sequential order.
Therefore, it is simply stated that they are applied "according to what is appropriate.
Specifically, regarding the statement that one arrives at the perception of non-delight in order to counteract four kinds of obstacles:
the perception of impermanence counteracts craving for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) throughout the three periods of time.
The perception of suffering cures laziness.
The perception of impurity, the perception of disenchantment, and the perception of food cure the fourth [hindrance], which is craving for flavors.
The perception that all worlds are not worth delighting in cures the fifth [hindrance], which is craving for the wonderful things of the world.
The five aforementioned contemplations are all practices of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) that lack specific remedies.
Regarding the contemplations of suffering and non-self as obstacles to the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*):
these two contemplations of emptiness and non-self are both the gateway of emptiness.
Having instead treated the pride of intellectual arrogance regarding the third [level], the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),

which manifests as the conceit of "I," one cultivates the perception of the signless (*animitta*) throughout the three realms in order to sever and eliminate the remaining latent afflictions (*anuśaya*).
That is to say, contemplating abandonment, dispassion, and cessation is termed the "three realms.
These three perceptions—abandonment and so forth—are collectively the gateway of signlessness (*animitta*).

As for cultivating the perception of the defects of sensual desires in order to counteract the longing for gain and offerings as well as sensual craving: [this is done] within the midst of all sensual desires.
The seventh and ninth [perceptions] are both craving for external objects;
because one regards the perception of their defects as a longing for livelihood and existence, one cultivates the perception of death.
These eighth and tenth [perceptions] both give rise to craving toward the internal body;
therefore, the perception of death (*maraṇasaṃjñā*) serves as their antidote.

Because they follow after false conceptualizations of the four types of sensual desire, one cultivates the perception of impurity (*aśubhasaṃjñā*) as the first, up to the perception of emptiness (*śūnyatāsaṃjñā*) as the last.
One cultivates the perception of a livid corpse and the perception of a bloated corpse in order to abandon craving for beautiful color;
one cultivates these to abandon craving for physical form.
Therefore, the contemplation on the process of eating and consuming, as well as the contemplation on the disintegration of the body, are cultivated as antidotes.
To sever craving for subtle tactile sensations, one cultivates the contemplation on skeletons and the contemplation on bone chains;
these serve as antidotes to craving for service and attendance.
Therefore, one cultivates the perception of a corpse as being without mind or consciousness, and as empty.

Furthermore, it should be understood that all these [perceptions], from the perception of a livid corpse up to the perception of emptiness, are subsumed within the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*).
These nine contemplations of perception are collectively the nine distinct types of meditation derived from within the general category of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, regarding the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) within this context, one should understand its characteristics as extending to the utmost limit of the Sphere of Total Purity (*śubhakṛtsna-āyatana*) and beyond.
This explains the preceding passage which, within the discussion on "immediate concomitance," cited the example that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth are likewise.
The sixth major section explains the Noble Eightfold Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) with one verse that sets forth its four gateways.
First, internal and external power;
second, distinctions of purity;
third, alternative formulations.

This concludes the end of the twenty-fourth fascicle, Part Two, of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā*. Appended after the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā* are the words of the Great Virtuous Dunlun of the Li Tang (Tang Dynasty).
Exerting his essence in yoga,
he composed this record of the treatise,
thereby manifesting the beauty of his prior cultivation.
He alone created these aggregates,
bringing them to completion as a great achievement.
As for one who is so petty and mediocre, what need is there for even a single word of praise?
However, this book exists in the world in only a few copies;
as for its preservation in secret mountains and ancient monasteries,
it is even rarer to be transmitted or encountered.
In the past, I earnestly requested a copy to be transcribed,
which I have reverently stored within my chest.
However, having been in circulation for many years,
the text has become corrupted and erroneous;
it is not without its regrets.
Later, when it was titled *The Original Text of the Treasury of Compassionate Mind*,
he collated and corrected it no fewer than three times.
Thereafter, he sighed to himself alone:
Why has this Dharma-treasure not spread so widely?
It is because we are selfish and scholars dread the hardship of copying it by hand.
Thus, out of humble consideration, I have devised a plan to print and distribute it.
Jue-sheng has humbly heard that Yue-shi polished the jujubes.
Thereupon, disregarding my own meager learning,
I have ventured to provide a national reading for the characters and phrases alongside [the text].
